summary: NEBULITH is a web app for exploring Earth, the Moon and Mars, and for studying how Earth locations can act as analogues for other worlds. It offers an interactive 3D globe with place search, a rover digital twin with live telemetry, a Research Lab for uploading documents, and saved studies. Analog discovery, comparison and real-elevation routes are planned. Built with React, TypeScript, Three.js, FastAPI and SQLite.
details:
NEBULITH: Project details

What it does and how it works

NEBULITH is a web app for exploring Earth, the Moon and Mars, and for studying how places on Earth can stand in as analogues for other worlds. Users spin an interactive 3D globe, switch between the three bodies, and search for a place by name or coordinates. A rover digital twin lets them pick a terrain profile (basalt, regolith, dunes or polar ice), set terrain height and ambient temperature, and watch a rover drive with live telemetry: battery, power draw, slope, pitch and roll, wheel slip and traction. A Research Lab lets users upload PDF, DOCX, CSV and XLSX files, build a source library and extract the locations mentioned in their documents. A mission workspace saves studies through a FastAPI and SQLite backend.

Benefits

Planetary exploration, location data, rover behaviour and research documents are in one place instead of scattered across tools.

It is easy to start with: it runs in a browser, with no specialist software needed.

Results are designed to stay traceable. The goal is that every value keeps its source, units and limits.

Intended impact

We want to make analogue research and mission thinking more accessible to students, early researchers and space enthusiasts. We also want to set an example of honest planetary tooling: no fake precision, no hidden assumptions, and no pretending a visual is a measurement. The roadmap covers analog discovery, side-by-side comparison, transferability analysis, and routes built on real elevation data.

Tools and technologies

Frontend: React 19, TypeScript 5.7, Vite 6, React Router 7, Three.js (globe and digital twin), Lucide icons, and MapLibre GL for the planned 2D map.

Backend: Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, SQLite.

Hardware: no special hardware. It runs on a standard computer in a browser.

What makes it creative?

It connects Earth-based analogue research to the rover’s behaviour in one workflow, which most tools treat separately.

The digital twin makes terrain and temperature tangible: change a slider and watch traction, slip and the rover’s own safety response change.

The interface is built like a mission-control dashboard, which makes the science feel approachable.

Design rules are part of the product. For example, missing data is shown as missing, never as zero, and an analogue is never called a twin.

Factors we considered

Scientific honesty: we separated the globe, the 2D map and the 3D terrain scene so a nice-looking visual isn’t mistaken for a measurement.

Data quality: units, resolution, coverage and provenance must stay attached to results. The current globe textures and procedural terrain are illustrative, and we say so.

AI limits: explanations must never replace calculations. The Research Lab’s Q&A currently runs in mock mode and is labelled that way.

Scope: we built a working foundation first (globe, twin, document library, studies) and staged the harder science work behind it.

Usability: a clear interface, familiar web tools, and an easy local setup.
